0.title: Skill for Living in the Fear of the Lord
0.essay:
Most of us know clever people who make a mess of their lives, and plain people who handle life remarkably well. The difference is not intelligence, education or experience alone. The Bible calls it wisdom.

Knowing how to live

A person can hold a doctorate and be a fool, and a person who never finished school can be wise. Wisdom is not how much you know. It is knowing how to live.

Scripture gives wisdom a great deal of space. Whole books are devoted to it: Proverbs, Job, Ecclesiastes, many psalms and the letter of James. Jesus taught in parables and proverbs, and ended his greatest sermon with a story about a wise builder and a foolish one. Paul prayed that believers would be “filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding” (Colossians 1:9). Wisdom is not an optional extra for unusually thoughtful Christians. It is part of ordinary obedience.

A person at the centre

The Bible’s teaching on wisdom has a surprise at its heart. Wisdom is not finally a set of principles but a person. Paul calls Jesus Christ “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), the one “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). To grow in wisdom is to grow in Christ.

A working definition

Biblical wisdom is the God-given skill of living well in God’s world: seeing life as God sees it, and then choosing, speaking and acting in a way that fits his character, his word and the situation in front of you. It begins with the fear of the Lord, it is learned from Scripture, it grows through prayer, counsel, correction and experience, and it shows itself in a humble and peaceable life.

The chapters

What Wisdom Is; Christ, the Wisdom of God; Two Ways: Wisdom and Folly; How Wisdom Grows; Wise and Foolish Lives in Scripture; Wisdom for Everyday Life; Passing Wisdom On; The Limits of Wisdom and the Rest of Faith; and Proverbs to Memorize, which gathers key proverbs on a single page to learn by heart. It belongs with the study on the Fear of the Lord, where wisdom begins.

1.title: What Wisdom Is: Skill for Living in God’s World
1.essay:
The Old Testament word usually translated “wisdom” is hokmah, and its range is wider than we might expect. It can describe a tailor or a metalworker.

Skill

When God gave Moses instructions for the priests’ garments, he said, “You shall speak to all the skillful, whom I have filled with a spirit of skill” (Exodus 28:3). “Skill” there is the word for wisdom. Bezalel, the craftsman of the tabernacle, was filled “with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship” (Exodus 31:3), and “ability” is the same word again. These were not priests or prophets. They cut stone, carved wood and wove cloth, and their wisdom was seen in well-made things used for the worship of God.

So wisdom is practical. It is not floating ideas but good work, rightly done, for God’s glory. A Christian nurse who treats patients with competence and kindness, or a mechanic who does honest work, is showing a kind of wisdom God gives and values. Wisdom belongs in the workshop, the kitchen and the office as well as the study.

The skill of making a life well

Biblical wisdom is the skill of making a life well: taking what God has said and living it out in the untidy details of real days — a marriage, a workplace, a budget, a conflict, a grief, a decision with no clear rule attached. Knowledge knows that God commands honesty. Wisdom knows how to be honest with a grieving friend, a difficult boss or a teenage son, and when to speak and when to wait.

The beginning

“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction” (Proverbs 1:7). This is the motto of Proverbs, set at the front door so every reader passes through it. The same truth is repeated in Proverbs 9:10, Psalm 111:10 and Job 28:28, as if Scripture wants to make sure we do not miss it. “Beginning” does not mean a first step you leave behind, but the foundation everything else stands on.

The fear of the Lord is not terror of a cruel master. It is reverent awe before the holy God who made us and to whom we will give account, an awe that leads to trust, worship and obedience. Wisdom starts there because God made the world and knows how it works. Trying to live well while ignoring him is like using a complicated machine after throwing away the maker’s instructions. So wisdom is first spiritual and only then practical. The wise person in the Bible is not mainly the one with good tips for life, but the one who has bowed before God and so begins to see everything else in its proper light.

Notice the other half of the verse. The opposite of the wise person is not the uneducated person but the one who will not be taught. In Scripture, folly is not a lack of brains. It is a moral choice, the refusal to let God and his word correct you.

Seek it like silver

Listen to the verbs a father uses in Proverbs 2: receive my words, treasure up my commandments, make your ear attentive, call out for insight, raise your voice for understanding, “seek it like silver and search for it as for hidden treasures” (Proverbs 2:4). Wisdom does not fall on the lazy. It is found by people who want it badly enough to dig. Yet the passage ends not with our effort but with God’s gift: “For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding” (Proverbs 2:6). Both are true. We search with all our heart, and when we find wisdom we discover that God was giving it all along. Wisdom is received from God, through his word, by people who come to him humbly. That is why the most gifted person can be a fool and the simplest believer wise.

Knowledge, obedience and character

Scripture values knowledge but never treats it as enough: “knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians 8:1). Knowledge is what you know; wisdom is knowing what to do with it before God and for the good of others.

Moses told Israel that keeping God’s law “will be your wisdom and your understanding in the sight of the peoples” (Deuteronomy 4:6). Wisdom and obedience are not two different things. A life ordered by God’s word is the wise life, and a life that drifts from it, however sophisticated, is the foolish one.

And James will not let wisdom stay in the head: “Who is wise and understanding among you? By his good conduct let him show his works in the meekness of wisdom” (James 3:13). True wisdom is meek. It does not need to win every argument or display how much it knows. Some of the wisest Christians you will ever meet are quiet people whose wisdom you notice only over years, in how they handle trouble, forgive wrongs and give counsel when asked. The loud and self-assured are often less wise than they sound.

Which question comes first?

Two people face the same news: a job offer in another city, with more money but less time for church and family. One asks only, “What will I gain?” The other asks, “What will this do to my soul, my marriage, my children and my service of Christ? What do the people who know me best think? What has God said about money, contentment and priorities?” Both may be intelligent. Only the second is beginning to think wisely, because only the second is starting with God.

When you face a decision, notice which question comes first in your mind. If it is “What do I want?”, you are beginning where folly begins. If it is “What would please God here?”, you are standing at the beginning of wisdom.

For reflection

How would you have defined wisdom before reading this? How does “skill for living” change that? What does it look like to fear God in ordinary life? Think of the wisest person you know: how much of their wisdom is knowledge, and how much character? Where do you most need practical, God-given skill right now?

2.title: Christ, the Wisdom of God
2.essay:
The Old Testament searches for wisdom. Job asks, “But where shall wisdom be found? And where is the place of understanding?” (Job 28:12). Proverbs pictures wisdom as a woman calling in the streets. Solomon was given wisdom beyond any king before him, and yet he finished badly.

Glimpsed, never embodied

The long story of Israel shows that even the wisest human beings could not live the wise life consistently. Wisdom was promised, sought and glimpsed, but never fully embodied. Then Jesus came.

As a boy he “increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man” (Luke 2:52). The eternal Son of God, in his true humanity, grew. He learned as a child learns; he listened and asked questions (Luke 2:46). If the sinless Son of God grew in wisdom over time, we should be patient with the slow work God is doing in us.

As a man he taught with such authority that crowds were astonished, and he silenced every trap his enemies set. He said of himself, “something greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42). The queen of Sheba had come from the ends of the earth with hard questions, and Solomon answered them all (1 Kings 10:1–3). Now the true King was walking the roads of Galilee, and his own generation did not come to listen. People still travel far, read widely and pay dearly for wisdom, while leaving the Gospels unopened on a shelf.

The foolishness of God

The deepest wisdom of God was revealed at the place that looked most foolish. “For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:22–24). Some want signs: show me power and I will believe. Others want wisdom: give me an argument that satisfies my mind on my terms. God gave neither on their terms. He gave a crucified Messiah. What changes is not the message but the eyes. Spiritual wisdom begins when God opens our eyes to see the cross as glory.

At the cross God did what no human wisdom could have imagined. He upheld his justice and saved sinners at the same time, by bearing the punishment himself in his Son.

Christ our wisdom

“And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30). “Because of him”: you are in Christ by God’s action, not your own cleverness. Paul has just reminded the Corinthians that “not many of you were wise according to worldly standards” (1 Corinthians 1:26). God delights to make the overlooked wise in Christ. And the four words belong together. Christ is not only the wise teacher who shows the way; he is the Saviour who makes us right with God, makes us holy and sets us free. Wisdom here is not a separate gift beside salvation; it is God’s whole saving plan, received in Christ. A believer who knows almost nothing else knows the wisest thing in the universe: that God saves sinners through his crucified and risen Son. Wisdom that does not lead you to his cross is not the wisdom of God.

So Christian wisdom is not first a technique but a relationship. To be united to Christ by faith is to have the wisdom of God as your own, and to spend the rest of your life learning to think and live like him.

All the treasures

In Christ “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). “Hidden” does not mean locked away from believers. It means stored up in Christ and nowhere else, like gold in a vault, so that anyone who wants them must come to him. The Colossians were being offered spiritual experiences, special knowledge and strict rules as the way to a deeper life. Paul’s answer was that you cannot go deeper than Christ. Every claim to a higher wisdom outside him is a step down, not up. The Christian life is a lifelong exploration of what you already have.

Proverbs 8

In Proverbs 8, wisdom speaks as a person who was with God before creation, “like a master workman” (Proverbs 8:30). Christians have read this in two main ways. Some take it as a direct description of the eternal Son before the incarnation. Others take it as a poetic picture of God’s own wisdom, personified to make it vivid, which the New Testament then shows to be fully embodied in Christ, through whom all things were made (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16).

The second reading is the more likely. The chapter is poetry about an attribute of God, and its language should not be pressed into a statement about the Son’s origin. In the fourth century some used “The LORD possessed me at the beginning of his work” (Proverbs 8:22) to argue that Christ was a created being, and the church rightly rejected that, because the Son is eternal God. But the line from Proverbs 8 to Christ is real: everything said there of God’s wisdom is perfectly true of him.

When the clever mock

A young believer at university is surrounded by impressive voices. Professors, authors and online commentators seem far cleverer than anyone at church, and some openly mock faith in a crucified Saviour. First Corinthians 1 was written for exactly this moment. The message of the cross has always sounded foolish to the clever. That is not evidence against it. Scripture says it is the shape God’s wisdom was always going to take, “so that no human being might boast in the presence of God” (1 Corinthians 1:29).

A practical habit: when you are unsure what wisdom looks like in a situation, ask how Jesus dealt with people in the Gospels — the proud, the broken, the hostile, the curious. He is not only the source of our wisdom but its clearest picture.

For reflection

Why do you think God revealed his wisdom through something that looks as foolish as the cross? Where are you tempted to look for wisdom outside Christ? How does it encourage you that Jesus “increased in wisdom”? Read Colossians 2:1–10: which treasures in Christ do you most need to explore?

3.title: Two Ways: Wisdom and Folly
3.essay:
The Bible presents life as a road with two ways. Psalm 1 sets the blessed man, whose “delight is in the law of the LORD” (Psalm 1:2), against the man who walks in the counsel of the wicked. Jesus ends the Sermon on the Mount with two builders. And Proverbs 9 pictures the choice as two women, each calling to passers-by.

Two invitations

Lady Wisdom has built her house, prepared a feast and sent out her servants. She is not a stern examiner but a generous host. And whom does she invite? “Whoever is simple … him who lacks sense” (Proverbs 9:4). She does not wait for people to become wise before inviting them; she calls those who know they need her. “Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight” (Proverbs 9:6). It is a picture of the gospel itself. God’s feast is spread for the needy, and the only requirement is to come.

Across the street, the woman Folly sits at her door, on the highest places of the town, just as Wisdom does. She calls the same people with the same words: “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” (Proverbs 9:16). Temptation rarely looks obviously evil. It imitates the good. But listen to her offer: “Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant” (Proverbs 9:17). Her appeal is that the thing is forbidden. And she does not tell her guests the truth: “But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol” (Proverbs 9:18). Sin always hides the ending. The wise person learns to ask, before going through any door, “Where does this road lead?”

“There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death” (Proverbs 14:12). Every day we walk down that street and hear both voices.

A cast of fools

Proverbs gives us a cast of foolish characters so that we can recognise them in ourselves. The simple person is naive and easily led, open to any voice. The fool has heard the truth but prefers his own way: “The way of a fool is right in his own eyes” (Proverbs 12:15). The scoffer mocks correction and laughs at serious things. And the sluggard always has a reason not to act. The simple can still learn. The fool and the scoffer have hardened themselves against learning.

Biblical folly is not low intelligence. Many brilliant people are fools in the Bible’s sense, and many ordinary people are wise. Folly is a heart that will not submit to God or receive correction.

No God, in the heart

“The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 14:1). He may never say it aloud. He may even go to church. But in his heart, where decisions are really made, he lives as if God were not there. This kind of atheism is not a philosophical position but a way of living: planning, spending, speaking and loving as if God did not exist. Paul quotes this psalm in Romans 3 to show that all of us by nature are fools in this sense. The wise are not those who were never fools, but those whom God has brought to their senses. That is why the Bible’s call to wisdom is always also a call to repentance and faith.

And there is hope for fools. Wisdom cries, “How long, O simple ones, will you love being simple?” (Proverbs 1:22), and promises to teach those who turn at her reproof. Every wise Christian was once a fool rescued by grace.

Two builders

Jesus’ two builders have one thing in common: both hear his words. The difference is not knowledge but obedience. “Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock” (Matthew 7:24); the other hears and does not do them. That is sobering for people who hear many sermons and read many books. Hearing is not building. And both houses face exactly the same storm. Wisdom does not protect us from trouble. It means that when trouble comes, our lives stand on the rock of Christ and his word, and the house does not fall. Scripture offers no neutral middle road. Every choice, however small, builds on one foundation or the other.

Two friends start work at the same time. One builds habits of Bible reading, prayer, church involvement, honest work and careful spending. The other drifts: Sundays are for rest, money is for enjoying, and God can wait until life settles down. For years there is little visible difference; both houses look fine in the sunshine. Then come the storms Jesus promised would come to both — illness, job loss, a marriage crisis, a death — and the difference between the foundations finally shows.

Folly looks like common sense

Lot looked at the well-watered plain near Sodom and chose it because it looked good (Genesis 13:10–11). Abraham let God choose for him. Lot’s choice made perfect sense by every worldly measure, and it cost him nearly everything. Folly often looks like common sense at the moment of decision.

Folly’s voice today often sounds like this: “Nobody will know.” “You deserve it.” “Everyone else does it.” “You can deal with God later.” Wisdom’s voice sounds like this: “God sees.” “What will this lead to?” “Who will this hurt?” “Seek first his kingdom.”

For reflection

Read Proverbs 9 aloud. What does Folly promise, and what does she hide? Which of the foolish characters — simple, fool, scoffer or sluggard — do you recognise most in yourself? Where are you hearing God’s word without doing it? In what part of your life might you be living as if “there is no God”, even while believing in him?

4.title: How Wisdom Grows
4.essay:
No one is born wise. Wisdom has to be gained, and Scripture is clear about how God usually gives it: through a few ordinary means, used faithfully over a long time.

We ask

“If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him” (James 1:5). James wrote to believers in the middle of trials, who did not know what God was doing or how to respond. He does not say, “Work it out yourself.” He says ask. And look at how God gives: generously, to all, and without reproach. He does not sigh at our ignorance or make us feel foolish for asking. A wise Christian is not someone who never feels lost, but someone who knows where to go when he does, and goes often.

James adds that we must ask “in faith, with no doubting” (James 1:6). That does not mean feeling certain about every detail. It means really trusting that God is good and wants to help, rather than hedging our bets between God and the world. And it is not a promise of new revelation — a voice or inner impression that settles our decisions for us. Scripture is sufficient to make us “complete, equipped for every good work” (2 Timothy 3:17). It is a promise that God will give the understanding we need to walk faithfully, through his word, through others and through his guiding hand in our circumstances. “The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps” (Proverbs 16:9).

We soak ourselves in Scripture

“The testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple” (Psalm 19:7). The sacred writings, Paul told Timothy, “are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 3:15). The psalmist makes a bold claim: God’s word made him wiser than his enemies, his teachers and the aged (Psalm 119:98–100). He is not boasting about his intelligence. He gives the reason each time: “for it is ever with me”; “for your testimonies are my meditation”; “for I keep your precepts”. The word was always with him, he thought about it deeply, and he obeyed it. That path is open to every believer, however young or ordinary. A Christian who rarely opens the Bible will rarely be wise.

We walk with the wise

“Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm” (Proverbs 13:20). Our companions shape us more than we realise. The verse does not say walking with the wise makes you feel wise, but that it makes you wise. Wisdom is caught as well as taught, in friendship, mentoring and the life of a local church. For parents it speaks to children’s friendships. For all of us it asks whose company we seek, and whose voices fill our screens.

King Rehoboam was given two sets of advice. The older men who had served his father counselled gentleness; the young men he had grown up with urged harshness. “But he abandoned the counsel that the old men gave him and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him” (1 Kings 12:8). The kingdom split in two. He chose his advisers by comfort and familiarity, not by wisdom.

We welcome correction

“Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid” (Proverbs 12:1). Proverbs is blunt. Few things reveal a fool faster than how he reacts when someone tells him he is wrong. Humility is the soil in which wisdom grows: “Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD, and turn away from evil” (Proverbs 3:7). Someone who thinks he is already wise has stopped growing.

We learn by practice and suffering

Mature believers are those “who have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil” (Hebrews 5:14). The picture is of an athlete whose skills have become second nature. At first you must think hard about every choice. Over time, as you practise obeying God’s word, you begin to sense quickly what is good and what is evil. There are no shortcuts. Wisdom is built one faithful decision at a time. And trials, James says, are part of how God makes us “perfect and complete” (James 1:4).

Above all, we remember that life is short: “So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom” (Psalm 90:12).

God could make us wise in an instant, but he usually does not. He works through his word, prayer, the church and the experiences of life. These are not substitutes for his work; they are how he works.

What asking looks like

A young couple are making a big decision about buying a house. They pray about it, which is good. But they also sit down with an older couple from church who have managed money well for decades, listen to hard questions about debt and commitments, read what Proverbs says about borrowing, and wait a month before signing. That is what asking God for wisdom usually looks like in practice: prayer joined with the word, counsel and patience.

A simple plan: read the chapter of Proverbs that matches the day of the month, for a year. Pray James 1:5 each morning about one specific situation. Find one older Christian whose life you admire and ask to meet regularly. And the next time someone corrects you, say “Thank you” before you say anything else.

For reflection

When did you last ask God specifically for wisdom about something? Read Psalm 119:97–104: what would it look like for God’s word to be “ever with” you? Who are the wise people you walk with, and which voices shape your thinking most? How did you respond the last time someone pointed out a fault in you?

5.title: Wise and Foolish Lives in Scripture
5.essay:
The Bible does not only teach wisdom in sayings. It shows it in lives. Its stories are full of people who acted wisely or foolishly at decisive moments, and their examples train us to recognise wisdom when we see it.

Joseph

Joseph was a slave and a prisoner for years before he stood before Pharaoh. He interpreted Pharaoh’s dreams, but he also gave a practical plan for surviving the famine, and Pharaoh said, “there is none so discerning and wise as you are” (Genesis 41:39). Pharaoh could explain it only by God: “Can we find a man like this, in whom is the Spirit of God?” (Genesis 41:38). Joseph had told him plainly, “It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer” (Genesis 41:16). His wisdom was not self-made, and he did not claim it was.

It included planning ahead and administering well, and later, forgiving his brothers with a deep grasp of God’s purposes: “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). True wisdom is often visible to unbelievers. A Christian who does good work, gives sound advice and keeps calm under pressure may find, like Joseph, that people outside the church sense something more than human ability at work, and that opens a door to point them to God.

Abigail

Abigail was married to a fool. Her husband Nabal insulted David, and David set out with four hundred men to kill every male in the household. Abigail acted quickly. She gathered gifts, met David on the road, and spoke with humility and courage, reminding him of God’s promises. And David, to his credit, saw God’s hand in it: “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you this day to meet me! Blessed be your discretion, and blessed be you, who have kept me this day from bloodguilt and from working salvation with my own hand!” (1 Samuel 25:32–33). Wise people make peace at personal risk. And wise people, like David here, are willing to be stopped by someone with less power than they have.

Imagine a woman caught between an angry husband and the neighbour he has offended. She does not shout, and she does not do nothing. She goes to the neighbour, apologises for the wrong, brings a gift and speaks honestly and graciously. Later, when her husband is calm, she tells him what she did. That is Abigail’s wisdom: quick, humble, courageous and peace-making.

Daniel

Daniel, an exile in a pagan court, refused to compromise his faith yet served the king with excellence. When the king ordered the execution of all the wise men, “Daniel replied with prudence and discretion” (Daniel 2:14), asked for time and went to pray with his friends. Earlier he had asked respectfully for vegetables instead of the king’s food (Daniel 1:8–16), looking for an honourable alternative before he had to make a stand. An employee asked to take part in something dishonest might do the same: request a meeting, propose an honest way to reach the same goal, pray quietly, and be ready to stand firm if she must.

The wise woman of Abel

When Joab besieged a town to catch a rebel, an unnamed wise woman called to him from the wall, spoke sensibly, and saved her whole city (2 Samuel 20:16–22). Scripture’s wise people include a slave who became a ruler, a wife in a hard marriage, an exile in a foreign government, a king and a woman whose name we never learn. Wisdom is not tied to rank, gender or position. It is given to those who fear the Lord, and the prophet foretold that the Spirit would rest on the coming King as “the Spirit of wisdom and understanding” (Isaiah 11:2).

Solomon

Solomon is the Bible’s great example of wisdom and its great warning. When God offered him anything he wanted, he asked for “an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil” (1 Kings 3:9). He did not ask for wealth, long life or the death of his enemies, and God was pleased. It is a model prayer for anyone with responsibility: parents, pastors, managers, teachers.

But one of the saddest verses in the Old Testament follows: “For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God” (1 Kings 11:4). The wisest man who ever lived, apart from Christ, ended up worshipping idols. It did not happen in a day but after years of small compromises with what God had commanded about kings and their wives (Deuteronomy 17:17). Great insight did not protect a divided heart. Wisdom must be lived, not merely possessed, and guarded by a whole heart renewed daily in repentance. None of us is too wise to fall.

A gifted Bible teacher, admired for years, slowly lets small compromises grow: an unguarded friendship, a habit of private self-indulgence, a refusal to be accountable. His gifts remain, but his heart drifts. Many ministries have ended this way. Solomon’s story is written so that none of us assumes our gifts will keep us faithful. And his son Rehoboam threw the kingdom away by listening to the wrong advisers. Wisdom must be kept as well as gained.

All point to Christ

Each wise figure is a partial picture. Joseph forgave and saved his brothers; Abigail stood between a wrathful king and the guilty; Daniel was faithful in exile; Solomon ruled in wisdom and peace. Christ does all of this perfectly, and never falls.

For reflection

Which of these — Joseph, Abigail, Daniel or the wise woman of Abel — inspires you most, and why? Is there a conflict around you that needs Abigail’s kind of courageous peacemaking? What small compromises could, over years, draw your heart away as Solomon’s was? How does each of them point to Christ?

6.title: Wisdom for Everyday Life
6.essay:
Much of the Bible’s wisdom literature is intensely practical. Proverbs speaks about the tongue, anger, money, work, friendship, family and the heart. It is not a rulebook that answers every situation in advance, but a training school that shapes how we see and respond to life.

Words

“A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). Easy to memorise, hard to practise. When someone speaks in anger, our instinct is to answer in kind, and a harsh word is like petrol on a fire. A soft answer is not weak or dishonest; it can still say hard things, but in a tone that lowers the temperature. Many family arguments, church conflicts and workplace disputes would end quickly if one person chose to answer softly. Usually the wise person is the one who goes first.

Wisdom listens before it speaks: “If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame” (Proverbs 18:13). And it knows when to stop: “When words are many, transgression is not lacking” (Proverbs 10:19).

Anger

“Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city” (Proverbs 16:32). Self-control is a greater victory than conquest. “Good sense makes one slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook an offense” (Proverbs 19:11). When a colleague takes credit for your idea, folly broods, gossips or retaliates. Wisdom remembers that verse, and if the matter is serious, raises it privately and calmly.

A father comes home tired to find that his teenager has broken a rule. Folly explodes at once. Wisdom pauses, asks what happened, listens to the whole story — “The one who states his case first seems right, until the other comes and examines him” (Proverbs 18:17) — keeps its voice low, and deals with the matter firmly but without humiliation. The rule is upheld and the relationship survives.

Money

“The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender” (Proverbs 22:7). Wisdom saves, plans, gives generously and avoids debt that enslaves. It counts the cost before it builds (Luke 14:28). A family wants a new car they cannot afford. Folly signs the loan because the monthly payment seems manageable. Wisdom counts the full cost and keeps the old car another year while saving.

Work

“Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise. Without having any chief, officer, or ruler, she prepares her bread in summer and gathers her food in harvest” (Proverbs 6:6–8). The sluggard is sent to learn from an insect. Wise people take initiative without needing someone to watch them, and they plan ahead, working while there is opportunity. Proverbs treats laziness not just as wasted time but as a form of folly that leads to poverty and shame.

Friendship

“Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27:6). A true friend tells you the truth even when it hurts. When a friend is making a decision that will harm him, folly stays silent to keep the peace. Wisdom risks the friendship to speak the truth in love.

The heart

Beneath all of these lies the heart. “Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life” (Proverbs 4:23). Words, anger, spending and work all flow from what we love and trust.

Reading proverbs wisely

Two proverbs sit side by side on purpose: “Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest you be like him yourself. Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes” (Proverbs 26:4–5). They do not contradict each other. Sometimes arguing with a fool on his terms drags you down to his level; sometimes silence leaves him proud in his error. Which is it? It depends. Wisdom is not a list of rules applied without thought, but the skill of knowing which truth fits which moment. That is why we need not only proverbs but a wise heart to use them. When someone posts an unfair attack on your faith online, folly fires back a clever, cutting reply. Wisdom asks whether a response will help or only feed the argument, and if it answers, answers with gentleness and respect.

Proverbs are not promises. A proverb states how life generally works in God’s world. A soft answer usually turns away wrath, but not every angry person will be calmed. Reading proverbs as unbreakable guarantees leads to confusion and false guilt.

Wisdom from above

“But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere. And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace” (James 3:17–18). Almost every mark is relational. “Open to reason” is striking: wise people can be persuaded; they listen and change their minds when they are wrong. Set beside it the wisdom that is “earthly, unspiritual, demonic”, marked by “bitter jealousy and selfish ambition” (James 3:14–15). You can tell which is at work by its fruit. Wisdom is measured not by how many arguments we win but by how much peace and righteousness grows around us.

Jesus told his disciples to be “wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matthew 10:16). Christian wisdom is not naive; it sees the world clearly and acts shrewdly, yet without guile. And it includes how we use our hours, screens and attention: “Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil” (Ephesians 5:15–16).

For reflection

Which area — words, anger, money, work, friendship or the heart — most needs God’s wisdom in your life now? Why does it matter that proverbs describe patterns rather than guarantees? Read James 3:13–18: which marks of wisdom from above are growing in you, and which are missing? What would a soft answer have looked like in your last conflict?

7.title: Passing Wisdom On: Parents and Children
7.essay:
Proverbs is written in the voice of a parent. Again and again it begins, “My son”, and it opens with a call to both parents: “Hear, my son, your father’s instruction, and forsake not your mother’s teaching” (Proverbs 1:8). The book itself is wisdom handed from one generation to the next.

Down the generations

In chapter 4 the father even tells how he learned it: “When I was a son with my father … he taught me” (Proverbs 4:3–4). Wisdom is meant to travel down the generations. Psalm 78 describes a chain of telling — fathers to children, and those children to theirs — “so that they should set their hope in God” (Psalm 78:7). God works through families and the church to carry the faith forward.

On your heart, then on theirs

God gave Israel this responsibility from the beginning: “And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise” (Deuteronomy 6:6–7). The order matters. Parents cannot pass on what they do not possess, and a child quickly sees whether God’s word is the real centre of a parent’s life or only a Sunday habit.

And notice where the teaching happens: at home, on the road, at bedtime and at breakfast. The main classroom for wisdom is ordinary family life. The best teaching is often unplanned — a conversation in the car, a question at bedtime, a prayer when bad news comes. Children learn far more from what they see their parents love, fear, laugh at and pray about than from any formal lesson.

One family turns the evening meal into a quiet school of wisdom. Once or twice a week they read a proverb together and ask one simple question: “Where did we see this today?” A child mentions a friend who answered back angrily and made things worse; another remembers a teacher who listened before she judged. Over the years the proverbs become part of the family’s ordinary language.

Instruction and discipline

Wise parenting holds two things together. There is instruction: telling children about God, explaining why his ways are good and showing them Christ. And there is discipline: correcting, setting boundaries and letting wrong choices bring consequences. “Folly is bound up in the heart of a child” (Proverbs 22:15); children do not drift into wisdom on their own.

Discipline mirrors God’s own fatherly care: “the LORD reproves him whom he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights” (Proverbs 3:12). To refuse it is not kindness but neglect: “Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him” (Proverbs 13:24). Christians read the rod passages in two main ways: some as permitting measured physical discipline of young children, given calmly and in love; others as a figure for firm correction of every kind. The first is the more likely reading of what the words meant, but the heart of these verses is not the instrument. It is consistent, loving correction that does not leave a child to himself (Proverbs 29:15).

Eli was a priest of God, yet God judged his house “because his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them” (1 Samuel 3:13). David did the same with Adonijah: “His father had never at any time displeased him by asking, ‘Why have you done thus and so?’” (1 Kings 1:6), and Adonijah grew up to grasp at his father’s throne. Both men were godly in many ways, and both failed to correct their sons. Passive parenting is not gentle parenting.

Never harsh

Yet discipline must never become harshness. “Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4). In Paul’s world fathers held almost unlimited power over their children, and he puts a limit on it. Constant criticism, unfair rules, broken promises, favouritism, mockery and outbursts of temper all provoke. “Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged” (Colossians 3:21). And the positive calling is “of the Lord”: Christian parents do not train children merely to be polite or successful, but to know and follow Christ.

A proverb, not a contract

“Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it” (Proverbs 22:6). This is probably the best-known verse on parenting, and it gives real hope. Habits, convictions and loves formed in childhood often last a lifetime. Yet it is a proverb, and must be read as Proverbs teaches: as a general truth about God’s world, not a guarantee that cancels a child’s own heart or God’s sovereign choice. Some children of godly homes wander for years, and some never return, and their parents are not thereby proved unfaithful. Parents should train with great hope and pray with even greater dependence, knowing that only God can turn a heart.

Parents whose grown child has turned from the faith often carry crushing guilt. Wisdom tells them three things. Confess real failures honestly to God and, where right, to the child. Refuse false guilt for the child’s own choices. And keep praying, loving and leaving the door open, as the father in Jesus’ parable kept watching the road (Luke 15:20).

Not only parents

This is not only for parents. Grandparents, aunts and uncles, Sunday school teachers, mentors and single Christians who invest in younger believers are all passing wisdom on. Timothy’s “sincere faith” lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5). Acts tells us his father was a Greek (Acts 16:1), with no sign that he shared their faith. These two women passed on faith in a divided home, and from childhood Timothy knew “the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation” (2 Timothy 3:15). Then Paul invested in him and called him “my true child in the faith” (1 Timothy 1:2).

An older single woman in a church takes a teenage girl out for coffee once a month, opens Proverbs with her, and listens. Years later that girl calls her the person who taught her how to follow Christ. No one who teaches a child Scripture should think the work is small.

For reflection

What wisdom did you receive from your parents or other older believers, and what do you wish you had been taught? Where in your ordinary week could God’s word be woven into conversation with the next generation? How does reading Proverbs 22:6 as a proverb change how parents carry their hopes and failures? Who is one younger person you could invest in?

8.title: The Limits of Wisdom and the Rest of Faith
8.essay:
Proverbs teaches that life in God’s world usually follows a pattern: diligence brings plenty, righteousness brings blessing, folly brings ruin. But the Bible also contains two other wisdom books that ask hard questions about that pattern.

Job’s friends

Job is about a righteous man who loses everything. His friends had a tidy theology: suffering comes from sin, so Job must have sinned. They applied a true principle to the wrong situation, and God rebuked them for it (Job 42:7). Most of what they said sounded wise. But their wisdom had no room for mystery, and they wounded a suffering man. The wisest thing they did was at the start, when they sat with him in silence for seven days (Job 2:13).

Job himself questioned God, and in the end confessed, “I have uttered what I did not understand, things too wonderful for me, which I did not know” (Job 42:3).

Wisdom cannot be dug up

Job 28 is a poem about miners digging deep into the earth for silver, gold and precious stones. People can reach the darkest places of the earth, but they cannot dig up wisdom, and it cannot be bought with gold. God alone knows where it is found. And when he speaks, he gives not a secret formula but a way of life: “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding” (Job 28:28). We may not understand everything God is doing, but we can always know what he wants us to do.

Under the sun

Ecclesiastes is just as honest. The Preacher observes that “in much wisdom is much vexation” (Ecclesiastes 1:18). He pursued wisdom harder than anyone, and concluded that “man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun … even though a wise man claims to know, he cannot find it out” (Ecclesiastes 8:17). Good people die young; the wicked prosper; the same end comes to all. Some things God has not revealed, and no amount of study will uncover them. Wisdom accepts this, content to know what God has revealed and to leave the rest with him: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us” (Deuteronomy 29:29).

A diligent worker loses her job while a dishonest colleague is promoted. Proverbs might seem to have failed. Ecclesiastes says this is exactly what life under the sun looks like. Wisdom does not pretend otherwise. It keeps working honestly, trusts that God sees, and waits for the day when every deed will be judged.

And the book does not end in despair: “The end of the matter; all has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man. For God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil” (Ecclesiastes 12:13–14). Life under the sun is not the whole story. The wise live in the light of eternity.

Three books, one wisdom

Proverbs, Job and Ecclesiastes do not contradict one another. Proverbs gives the normal pattern of God’s world. Job shows that a righteous person may suffer for reasons hidden in heaven. Ecclesiastes shows that life under the sun, viewed without God, is vapour. Together they give a wisdom that is confident and humble at once.

Do not lean on your own understanding

“Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths. Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD, and turn away from evil” (Proverbs 3:5–7). These verses are often quoted at times of decision, but they are also about the limits of wisdom. Even the book that most celebrates wisdom tells us not to lean on our own understanding. That does not mean “don’t think”. It means don’t rest your whole weight on your understanding, as if it could carry you. Lean on the Lord. The promise is not that he will explain everything but that he will guide those who trust him, even when they cannot see far ahead. And self-confident wisdom is folly in disguise.

The cross and Job’s longing

Job longed for someone to stand between him and God: “There is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both” (Job 9:33). In Christ, the righteous sufferer has come. Jesus suffered not for his own sin but for ours, and the worst event in history became the greatest good. When our suffering makes no sense, the cross assures us that God’s wisdom is at work in ways we cannot yet see.

A faithful Christian couple lose a child. Well-meaning friends offer explanations: God needed another angel; everything happens for a reason you will soon see; perhaps there is sin to deal with. Like the words of Job’s friends, these often hurt more than they help. Wisdom sits with the grieving, prays, brings meals and says little. It does not claim to know why. It points gently to the God who suffered in Christ and has promised to wipe away every tear.

Where wisdom ends

Paul spent eleven chapters of Romans explaining the gospel and God’s plan for Jews and Gentiles. At the end of the most careful argument in the Bible, he does not say, “Now you understand everything.” He bursts into worship: “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Romans 11:33). That is where all true wisdom ends: not in pride at how much we know, but in praise of the God whose wisdom is infinitely greater. The wisest response to what we cannot understand is not to stop believing but to rest in the God who does understand. The wisest Christian is the one most amazed by God.

For reflection

Have you ever applied a true principle to the wrong situation, as Job’s friends did? Read Ecclesiastes 12:9–14: how does the ending change the way you read the rest? What in your life right now does not make sense, and what would trusting God in it look like? How does the cross help you trust God’s wisdom when you cannot trace his ways?

9.title: Proverbs to Memorize
9.essay:
Twenty-four proverbs, three for each of eight themes, chosen to carry the wisdom of this study into everyday life. Learn one a week, and in six months you will have them all.

The fear of the Lord

“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction” (Proverbs 1:7).

“Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding” (Proverbs 3:5).

“Every word of God proves true; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him” (Proverbs 30:5).

Pride and humility

“Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18).

“When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with the humble is wisdom” (Proverbs 11:2).

“Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).

Words

“A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1).

“If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame” (Proverbs 18:13).

“Gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the body” (Proverbs 16:24).

Anger and self-control

“Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city” (Proverbs 16:32).

“Good sense makes one slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook an offense” (Proverbs 19:11).

“Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offenses” (Proverbs 10:12).

Friends and counsel

“Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm” (Proverbs 13:20).

“Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another” (Proverbs 27:17).

“Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27:6).

Money and work

“Honor the LORD with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your produce” (Proverbs 3:9).

“The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender” (Proverbs 22:7).

“Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed” (Proverbs 19:17).

Plans and the future

“Commit your work to the LORD, and your plans will be established” (Proverbs 16:3).

“Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand” (Proverbs 19:21).

“Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring” (Proverbs 27:1).

The heart and character

“Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

“A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold” (Proverbs 22:1).

“The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe” (Proverbs 29:25).

Why memorise, and how

“I have stored up your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 119:11). A proverb learned by heart is there at the moment of temptation, anger or decision, when there is no time to look anything up. Proverbs were written short so that they could be remembered. And remember the lessons of this study as you learn them: they describe how God’s world usually works, not mechanical promises, and they all stand on the first one — wisdom begins with the fear of the Lord and is found in Christ, the wisdom of God.

A simple method: write the week’s proverb on a card and keep it by the kitchen sink, on the car dashboard or as your phone’s lock screen. Say it aloud each morning. By Saturday, try it without looking, and every few weeks review the earlier ones. Learn them as a family, a couple or a small group; children often memorise faster than adults and enjoy testing their parents. A proverb shared around the table soon becomes part of a household’s language: “Remember — a soft answer.”

For reflection

Which theme do you most need this year? Start with those three proverbs. Which proverb do you already find yourself recalling in daily life, and how has it helped? Who could you learn these with, so that you encourage and test one another?
